4.2.3 Street wall

Together with the public domain, the street wall with active ground floor frontage is the built element that shapes the way most of the city is experienced. The street wall provides spatial enclosure and must operate in concert with other street walls or podiums to form a satisfying and rich experience of the public spaces of the city for the community. Interruptions or erosions of the street wall generally work to undermine the vitality and definition of the street wall and are not favoured.

Objectives

  • O1. To ensure that the visual relationship between the street and public space is reinforced.
  • To design the street wall to achieve fine grain modulation to create visual interest and variety while ensuring for consistency in streetscape character.
  • O3. To create a vertical rhythm and visual interest to reduce the scale of building mass.

To implement an articulation zone within podiums and facades to allow architectural form to develop.

Principles

  • P1. Street wall design should reflect the context and interface with a particular street typology.
  • P2. Design the street wall to provides appropriate scale, material quality and detail.
  • P3 Minimise large expanses of inactive frontage.
  • P4. Retain and sensitively integrate existing heritage and historic shopfronts into new development.

Controls

  • C1. Street wall heights must be consistent with Figure 45. For Council to consider a variation to a street wall height a development application must include a streetscape analysis that demonstrates a more appropriate street wall height. Submissions must include:

(a) The street wall elevation at 1:500 scale in context showing existing buildings on the block;

(b) A detailed street wall elevation at 1:200 scale including the buildings immediately adjacent.

  • C2. Where a street frontage length of an individual building exceeds 45m in length, it is to appear broken into two or more buildings each with different architectural characters. This outcome could be achieved through the following articulation design considerations or through other alternative design considerations to the reasonable satisfaction of Council:

(a) Podiums measuring greater than 45-70m in length are divided into two or more vertical elements.

(b) Vertical elements must be separated by indentations at a scale legible in the street and use a varied architectural expression and materiality.

(c) In cases where there is a range of heights in a street wall, prioritise the lower range along laneways, pedestrian links, and areas with high pedestrian activity.

  • C3 . Where there are existing historic pre 1950 shopfront street walls, such as along the Canterbury Road frontage, these shopfronts should be sensitively be integrated into new development to the satisfaction of Council.
  • C4. Where the adjacent built form context is lowerscale and not anticipated to change,development must provide a transition to the lower scaled built form and include appropriate articulation to fi t with the context.
  • C5. For sites including or adjacent to heritage items, development must transition the scale and height of the development and provide adequate separation and appropriate articulation to respect the scale established by the historic or existing context.

Figure 43: A four storey street wall defines the street edge, Breese by Breathe architects, photo by Tom Ross

  • C6. Datums derived from listed heritage buildings on the site or on an adjoining property - that is, the heights of the main ridgelines (or parapets in the case of commercial buildings), top plates/eaves level (or awnings of commercial buildings) and ground floor levels (street or natural ground levels)-must be used to ensure composition of height and scale is visually harmonious.

To create opportunities for tree canopy, planting and outdoor open space on podiums.

4.3.1 Residential ground floor frontage

Objectives

  • O1. To establish new canopy trees within setbacks that contribute to the character of the street and provide residents amenity and privacy.

To provide ownership and identity to residents by providing individual entries along the ground floor frontage out to the public domain.

  • O3. To provide for surveillance of public and publicly accessible space.

To encourage detailed attention to the design and to selection of materials at the lower level of residential buildings.

Principles

  • P1. Provide individual courtyards to ground floor apartments.
  • P2. Existing and proposed tree canopy should be contained within front setbacks to provide residents amenity and privacy.

Controls

  • C1. The front setback area must allocate a minimum of 3 metres from the boundary for deep soil landscaping. Canopy trees must be planted in this area 2.5 metres away from structures to achieve at least 12 metres mature height and spread, at the rate of 1 canopy tree for every 12 lineal metres of frontage
  • C2. Where a front setback is 3 metres width, the basement car parking must sit under the building footprint to allow for the deep soil zone. Where the setback is 6 metres, the basement can encroach 2 metres into the front setback.

4.3.2 Active Street frontage and edges

There are three areas where active street frontages are located within the Local Centre. These include Robert Street, Canterbury Square in Jeffrey Street South and the active edge in Canterbury South onto Lesley Muir Reserve. These active street frontage are identified in the LEP. Separately to the active street frontages are active edges. An active edge is secondary to an active street frontage.

Active street frontages must have a character similar to a traditional 'high street' and have many individual narrow shopfronts with services located away from the frontage. There are no large format stores and there is an intensity of activity.

Active uses include retail, customer service areas, cafes and restaurants, and other uses that involve pedestrian interest and interaction. Outdoor dining areas may also contribute to active street frontages in appropriate circumstances.

The active edges located on Canterbury Road could be business uses and have less activity than an active street frontage. Pierson Lane uses are more active as they are located on the edge of Canterbury Square.

Objectives

  • O1. To encourage finer grained narrow frontages to create varied experiences that provide views into and out of shops.

To ensure that Robert and Jeffrey Street South have a high quality and engaging public realm.

  • O3. To ensure that the interface and amenity of Canterbury Road is improved for pedestrians.

To encourage people to linger and enjoy public space.

  • O5. To ensure that building services do not dominate the pedestrian experience and are designed as an integrated part of the building form.
  • O6. To ensure ground floor active street frontage and edges are pedestrian oriented, have a high standard of design and add vitality to streets.
  • O7. To create opportunities to enjoy the positive aspects of climate and shield people from the negative such as wind, rain and heat.

To provide secondary edges that create vitality and interest.

Principles

  • P1. Vehicle entries are located away from key pedestrian areas.
  • P2. Awnings are to be used along active street frontages and edges.
  • P3. Shopfronts utilise lighting in the evenings when people are using public space for safety and activation.

Controls

  • C1. The location of active street frontages and active edges are shown on the Figure 54.
  • C2. Active edges should be provided on Canterbury Road and Pierson Lane.
  • C3. Vehicle access and loading should be located away from active street frontages and primary pedestrian areas. Service lanes priorities vehicles over pedestrians between the hours of 10pm to 7am.
  • C4. Awnings are to be provided to active frontages and extend 3m over the footway to provide protection from weather and hot sun. Awnings must:

(a) Integrate with the built form;

  • (b) Not be double height;

(c) Be non-reflective and not glazed

(d) Be harmonious with adjacent awnings and gutters and ensure downpipes and lighting are recessed and integrated with the building.

4.5 Materials and finishes

Buildings in our cities need to be comprised of low maintenance, robust and quality materials that will last the test of time. Canterbury Local Centre's heritage buildings demonstrates the success of this approach and how it provides Canterbury with its own special character. The many heritage items and historic shopfronts within the Local Centre create the opportunity to reference the past and to knit new development into the built environment. These materials include face brick and masonry.

Objectives

  • O1. To ensure high-quality materials and finishes seen in Canterbury's heritage and historic pre 1950 buildings is used throughout new development, with an emphasis on the ground floor, to enhance the pedestrian experience.

To ensure material selection and finishes are robust, have longevity, are low maintenance and contribute to beautiful buildings.

  • O3. To ensure Canterbury's heritage is reflected in the treatment of new development.

Principles

  • P1. Primarily use face brickwork, masonry and off form concrete.
  • P2. Have a higher ratio of solid to void in facades in response to heritage.
  • P3. Insert fine detailing through the use of timber, copper and metal.
  • P4. Create simplicity through the selection a common language of materials and finishes, rather than selecting many and creating visually complexity.

Controls

  • C1. Buildings must include durable single finish material finishes such as masonry, face brick and/or off form concrete. Painted cement render or similar painted finishes and Aluminium Composite Panel Cladding (e.g. Alucobond) must not be used. The use of glazing is not supported for awning construction or for parapet edges on rooftops.
  • C2. Elevate the pedestrian experience at street level through fine grained detailing using brickwork and provide details using copper, tiles and tactile surfaces.

4.6 Rooftop and podium communal open space

Principles

  • P1. Include well designed shade structures constructed of low maintenance natural materials for shading to seating areas and for trees and landscape for protection from summer sun and UV.
  • P2. Design spaces that people want to linger in due to the provision of shade or winter sun, landscape and facilities for passive socialisation.

Controls

  • C1. Building rooftops that are designated communal open space areas must be designed to include:

(a) Fixed seating in areas with shade and solar access, where appropriate.

(b) Accessible toilet facilities.

(c) Structures for rain protection and sun shading.

(d) A BBQ/food preparation area with a sink that is universally accessible

(e) Watering systems for proposed landscaping, and

Objectives

  • O1. Ensure that rooftops achieve good amenity standards for residents.

Encourage the use of rooftops for passive recreation and communal uses.

  • O3. Design rooftops to minimise the urban heat island impacts by using landscaping species suitable for windy and dry conditions and by providing shade structures.
  • Ensure rooftop open spaces are designed to promote the use of water and energy collected on site.
  • O5. Ensure balustrades around rooftop communal spaces are integrated into the design of the space and contributes to the overall appearance.
  • O6. Ensure harness anchor points are considered and integrated into the design where required for maintenance works to green roofs and walls.

(f) Stormwater management and disposal.

  • C2. Any rooftop structures are to be included in the maximum height of building permitted for the site within CBLEP 2023. The height is to be shown in the Development Application drawings.
  • C3. Any proposed communal open space located on the building podium and/or rooftop is to: (a) Be consolidated into a useable area with a minimum width of 6m and a minimum area of 36m².

(b) Be located so that solar access is provided for users of the open space.

(c) Be designed to a high quality and allow for landscaping and seating.

  • C4. Roof tops are to be structurally sound and have the capacity to support planting and adequate drainage.

C5. Communal open spaces must be designed to:

a) Accommodate both passive and active recreational uses, including clearly defined quiet or passive areas for relaxation and social interaction; and

b) Include designated children's play spaces that incorporate age-appropriate features such as swings, play equipment, landscaped mounds, and other interactive elements.

The functionality, layout, and design quality of communal open spaces must be clearly demonstrated in the submitted architectural and landscape plans.

SECTION 5 GENERAL PROVISIONS

5.1 Dwelling mix and flexible housing

Objectives

  • O1. Provide a range of housing types and sizes to support diverse households including single person families, multi-generational families, group households, students and seniors.

Ensure for equitable access to new housing opportunities for culturally and socio-economically diverse groups.

  • O3. Encourage the design of buildings that are adaptable and flexible to accommodate residents' changing housing needs over their lifetimes.

Controls

  • C1. The following dwelling mix is required for residential flat buildings and shop top housing developments containing 20 or more dwellings:
  • (a) Studio: between 5-10%.
  • (b) 1 bedroom: between 10-30%.
  • (c) 2 bedroom: between 40-75%.
  • (d) 3 or more bedroom: minimum 10%.
  • C2. The dwelling mix requirements may be altered only if the development serves the purpose of public housing or if the applicant represents a community housing or non-profit organisation.
  • C3. Within residential flat buildings, bedrooms should be located within apartments that have level access to adjoining communal space to provide accessibility to that space for disabled, elderly people and families with children.

5.2 Parking

Objectives

  • O1. Promote sustainable transport and limit vehicular movements by restricting private parking and facilitating increasing access to, and use of, communal modes of transport within the Local Centre. Require a lower minimum parking rate in the Local Centre 'Core' near the Canterbury Metro station, with a slightly higher minimum parking rate outside of the Local Centre 'Core' to minimise a reliance on private motor vehicle trips.

Principles

  • P1. Encourage basement vehicular parking instead of at-grade or above ground parking.
  • P2. Provide flexibility for the efficient use of car parking in development by allow off-site users to use car parking.
  • P3. Where provided, design above ground car parking so that it can be adapted to alternate uses over time.
  • P4. Consider the location of car park and service vehicle entrances and exits to ensure the amenity of public domain is maintained and improved where possible.
  • P5. To facilitate adaptation of car parking to other uses in the long term, above ground car parking is to remain as part of the common property and not part of, or attached to, individual strata units.

Controls

  • C1. All car parking within the Local Centre must be provided in accordance with the rates as specified in Table 8 and Figure 63. If a land use is not included in Table 8, the car parking rates in Chapter 2 Chapter 3.2 of the CBDCP 2023 will apply.

5.3 Underground floor space

Objectives

  • O1. To facilitate large floorplate uses underground, while maximising activation and permeability at street level.

Principles

  • P1. Uses permitted for underground floor space include uses that generally require large floor areas, including neighbourhood supermarkets, larger floorplate retail premises over 1000m² GFA, gym and entertainment facilities.
  • P2. Larger sites that can accommodate the above mentioned uses and demonstrate improved streetscape and public domain impacts.
  • P3. The underground uses should not go beyond the building footprint to ensure opportunities for deep soil planting and open space in setback areas are maintained.
  • P4. Entries to the underground floor space should have an appropriate, active, ground floor frontage.

Controls

  • C1. The basement levels used must have a minimum floor to ceiling height of 3.7 metres.
  • C2. The basement levels used must be the upper-most basement levels, closest to ground floor.
  • C3. The floor space is not used for the purposes of car parking.
  • C4. Does not result in the relocation of car parking at street level.
  • C5. Is located on a site with a minimum site area of no less than 3,000m².
  • C6. Any proposed or existing underground floor space is in addition to the maximum Floor Space Ratio for that site under the Canterbury-Bankstown Local Environmental Plan 2023 and any relevant applicable SEPPs. Any existing underground floor space on a site counts towards the maximum 1:1 underground floor space permitted.

5.4. Sustainability

5.4.2 Urban cooling and environmental sustainability

Overview

Urban heat or the Urban heat Island effect refers to the higher temperatures experienced in urban areas compared to rural or natural areas. As more development occurs, the build-up of heat in the environment occurs through heat being trapped in streets, increased hard surfaces, reduced vegetation and heat from air conditioning units.

Objectives

  • O1. To reduce the contribution of development to urban heat.
  • O2. To improve comfort for residents, workers and visitors in the local urban environment.
  • O3. To improve the passive comfort of dwellings and reduce the reliance on mechanical systems for amenity.
  • O4. To reduce the greenhouse gas emission release to the atmosphere through leakage, or improper disposal, of synthetic refrigerant gases with high Global Warming Potential (GWP).

Figure 64. The Langston Sydney, NSW, by Architectus (Source: Brett Broadman).

Controls

  • C1. Glazing in the external facade of an enclosed balcony or wintergarden must have a solar absorption of less than 10%.
  • C2. Solar absorption of glazing must be marked on plans, and verified through inclusion of window specifications with DA.
  • C3. All new air conditioning and refrigeration equipment are to use refrigerants with a GWP of less than 10 if the equipment can be supplied on similar terms to conventional systems. Confirmation prior to the release of the construction certificate is required.
  • C4. Solid fuel heating and cooking systems are not permitted in any development.
  • C5. Gas cooktops, gas ovens or gas internal space heating systems are not permitted in any residential development. Instead, electric systems must be installed and clearly marked on development application plans.
  • C6. Basement carparks must be contained within building footprints and allow for deep soil beneath forecourts and courtyards for large canopy tree planting.

The compliance of a Development Application with the controls in 5.4 is to be shown on the drawings and plans submitted with the Development Application and included in the Statement of Environmental Effects.

5.4.2 Reduction of the Urban Heat Island Effect

Objectives

  • O1. To minimise the reflection of solar heat downward from the building façade into private open space or the public domain.
  • O2. To reduce the contribution of development to urban heat and to improve user comfort in the local urban environment.
  • O3. To avoid or minimise the impact of heat rejection from air conditioning and refrigeration systems on the urban heat island effect and user comfort in private open space and the public domain.

The compliance of a Development Application with the controls in 5.4 is to be shown on the drawings and plans submitted with the Development Application and included in the Statement of Environmental Effects.

Controls

  • C1. The extent of the vertical façade of street walls (or if no street wall, as measured from the first 12 metres from the ground plane) that comprise Reflective Surfaces must demonstrate a minimum percentage of shading as defined in Table 7 as calculated at the relevant time of year in Table 9 and Table 10.
  • C2. The extent of the vertical façade of the tower (above the street wall or if no street wall, as measured above the first 12 metres from the ground plane) that comprise Reflective Surfaces must demonstrate a minimum percentage of shading as defined in Table 8 as calculated at the relevant time of year in Table 9 and Table 10.
  • C3. Compliance with C1 and C2 above is demonstrated on 21 December on the eastfacing façade at 10 AM, northeast and southeast facing façade at 11.30 AM, north-facing façade at 1 PM, northwest and southwest facing façade at 2.30 PM and the west-facing façade at 4 PM as shown in Table 9.
  • C4. Compliance with C1 and C2 above is demonstrated on 21 July on the northeastfacing façade at 10 AM, north northeast facing façade at 11.30 AM and 1 PM, and northwest facing façade at 2.30 PM and 4 PM as shown in Table 10.
  • C5. Shading may be provided by:
  • External feature shading with non-reflective surfaces.
  • Intrinsic features of the building form such as reveals and returns.
  • Shading from vegetation such as green walls, where requirements for upkeep is covered by a positive covenant.
  • C6. Where it is demonstrated that shading cannot be achieved in accordance with C1C4, development must provide:
  • A maximum external solar reflectance as defined in Table 8 is required for all Reflective surfaces;
  • Applicants must provide elevations illustrating facade surface areas, indicating the location of any shading devices and external finishes, and the solar reflectance value of the cladding;
  • Applicants must submit technical information that verifies the solar reflectance value of the cladding; and
  • Additional deep soil requirements to offset and reduce urban heat. The additional requirements will be determined by Council on a case by case basis.
  • C1. Shadow diagrams must be submitted with the development application quantifying the extent of shading at 10 AM, 11.30 AM, 1 PM, 2.30 PM and 4 PM on 21 December and 21 June for each relevant façade. Shadows from existing buildings, structures and vegetation are not considered in the calculations. These shadow diagrams are required in addition to, and not instead of, the requisite shadow diagrams to assess solar amenity and compliance with ADG requirements. Note: Refer to Table 9 and Table 10 for sun angles corresponding to shading reference times. Calculation of RSR for each relevant façade must also be submitted with the Development Application.
  • C2. Where surfaces on rooftops or podiums are used for communal open space or other active purposes, the development must demonstrate at least 50% of the accessible roof area complies with one or a combination of the following:
  • Be shaded by a shade structure, or/and;
  • Be shaded by a solar panel or/and;
  • Be covered by vegetation consistent with the controls on Green Roofs or Walls or/and
  • Provide shading through canopy tree planting, to be measured on the extent of the canopy cover 2 years after planting.

  • C1. Where surfaces on rooftops or podiums are not used for private or public open space, for solar panels or heat rejection plant, the development must demonstrate the following:
  • Materials used have a minimum solar reflectivity index (SRI) of 82 if a horizontal surface or a minimum SRI of 39 for sloped surface greater than 15 degrees.
  • 75% of the total roof or podium surface be covered by vegetation.
  • A combination of (a) and (b) for the total roof surface.
  • Applicants must provide a plan illustrating all roof surface areas, indicating the location of any green roofs, flat mounted PV panels, and the SRI value of the roofing.
  • Applicants must submit technical information that verifies the SRI performance of roofing.
  • C2. Residential apartments within a mixed-use development or residential flat building must incorporate efficient heating, ventilation and cooling systems which reject heat from a centralised source on the upper-most roof.
  • C3. No heat rejection units shall be located on the street wall frontage on the primary street.

5.4.3 Energy efficient (BASIX affected buildings)

Objectives

  • O1. Promote sustainable development which uses energy efficiently and minimises non-renewable energy usage during the construction and use of buildings.
  • O2. Ensure all new developments to actively contribute to the collective effort of reducing energy consumption throughout the Precinct.
  • O3. Decrease dependency on the main grid energy supply within the Precinct by implementing alternative energy sources and strategies.

Controls

  • C1. For developments not covered by BASIX, compliance with the energy efficiency provisions of the Building Code of Australia (Section J) is mandatory. A Section J report, along with annotated plans demonstrating compliance with fabric and service requirements, must be submitted.
  • C2. All development not subject to BASIX must issue documentation from a suitably qualified consultant is to be submitted with Development Applications demonstrating the measures that will be used to achieve the relevant energy efficiency scheme rating. Evidence of a formal commitment agreement or registration with the relevant scheme administrator is required to be submitted prior to the issuing of a construction certificate.
  • C3. All new developments must future proof the integration of smart technologies for the purposes of monitoring energy usage (e.g. Lighting, heat, ventilation and air conditioning).
  • C4. Verification of energy target achievement requires the submission of a signed Commitment Agreement from the National Australian Built Environment Rating System (NABERS).
  • C5. Targets for mixed-use developments must be tailored to the specific mix and proportion of land uses, determined on a site-specific basis and at the discretion of the Council.

5.4.4 Water efficiency

Objectives

  • O1. Reduce the consumption of drinking water.
  • O2. Increase the amount of water harvested from rainwater and urban stormwater runoff for use.
  • O3. Increase resilience to the impacts of water scarcity by providing sustainable alternative water supplies.
  • O4. Decrease the technical and financial barriers to retrospective upgrades to buildings to connect to future non drinking water supply infrastructure.

Controls

  • C1. All new developments must include submetering and future proof for smart technologies to minimise water consumption.
  • C2. Cooling towers must be designed in accordance with best practice guidelines to reduce water consumption.
  • C3. All development not subject to BASIX will need to incorporate the following watersaving measures:
  • Plumbing fixtures are to meet minimum Water Efficiency Labelling and Standards (WELS) Scheme Standards including 4 star rated showerheads, 4 star rated toilet cisterns, 5 star rated urinals and 6 star rated water tap outlets.
  • Appliances (dishwashers, clothes washers etc) are to be 5 stars (WELS Scheme) or better rated for water use efficiency.
  • C4. All development not subject to BASIX must issue documentation from a suitably qualified consultant is to be submitted with development Applications demonstrating the measures that will be used to achieve the relevant water efficiency scheme rating. Evidence of a formal commitment agreement or registration with the relevant scheme administrator is required to be submitted prior to the issuing of a construction certificate.
  • C5. Verification of energy target achievement requires the submission of a signed Commitment Agreement from the National Australian Built Environment Rating System (NABERS).
  • C6. Targets for mixed-use developments must be tailored to the specific mix and proportion of land uses, determined on a site-specific basis and at the discretion of the Council.

5.4.5 Electric Buildings

Objectives

  • O1. To minimise the reliance on the consumption of fossil fuels in new development.
  • O2. To prevent indoor pollutants associated with combustion.

Controls

  • C1. All new mixed-use development, residential development, commercial premises, tourist and visitor accommodation, health services facilities and educational establishments are to use only electricity for all energy requirements associated with normal operations.
  • C2. The use of fossil fuels for any purpose is not to exceed 1% of the projected annual energy demand for the building. **

* Note: BASIX certification for residential developments at a DA stage must not rely on gas for heating or hot water to comply with Control C1.

** Note: This control excludes emergency services and emergency infrastructure such as pumps and generators utilised in the case of emergencies (flood, fire, etc). 1% of projected annual energy demand for fossil fuels allows for the use of diesel for standby generation.

5.4.6 Solar energy requirements

Objectives

  • O1. Maximise the on-site collection of renewable energy.
  • O2. Minimise the consumption of electricity generated from non-renewable resources.

Controls

  • C1. Development must include the installation of a solar PV system of no less capacity than:
  • For sites with multiple electricity meters; rooftop photovoltaic (solar) panel system is connected to the common meter and the system is sized to offset 90-100% of estimated base building maximum demand.
  • For sites with a central electricity meter; the rooftop photovoltaic (solar) panels systems is sized to offset 30% of estimated maximum demand.
  • C2. With any DA plans submitted, the roof plan must show the area(s) allocated to PVs and necessary access requirements for cleaning and routine maintenance. PV solar panels must be setback at least 2m from the edge of the build roof or parapet.

SECTION 6 KEY SITES

6. Key Sites

Overview of Key Sites

The following sites have been identified as having a pivotal role in the realisation of the vision and objectives for the Canterbury Local Centre. The development of the key sites will be a catalyst for further development within the Local Centre and present an opportunity for precedent examples of design excellence, Connection to Country and the reflection of Canterbury's history and heritage through building form and materiality. The development on key sites will share a common language that is placed based.

To ensure for optimal outcomes for Canterbury and an efficient process for applicants, it is essential to engage with Council early in the Development Application process. Council will have an expectation to see detailed analysis of site, context and an understanding of the Aboriginal and European history of Canterbury.

To ensure for a 'fine grained' approach to key sites, Council encourages the subdivision of large sites into smaller lots that are contextual to site. If this cannot be achieved, then a variety of different buildings should be introduced of varying architectural character, scale and height to provide individual identity for residents and visitors.

Objectives

  • O1. Ensure that development is unique to the character, climate and demographic of Canterbury Local Centre.
  • O2. Achieve Design Excellence, create inspirational key sites with high quality innovative architecture that are sustainably built, reference Canterbury's history and heritage, offer community benefit, provide new publicly accessible and private spaces that contribute positively to Canterbury's sense of place and its skyline.
  • O3. Ensure that the principles of Connecting to Country are enshrined and represented in these sites.
  • O4. Ensure development does not compromise or reduce solar access to parks.
  • O5. Integrate laneways, expand the public domain, improve pedestrian and cyclist permeability and connect to existing and new open space.
  • O6. Provide for a range of heights on key sites to create an interesting and diverse skyline.
  • O7. Ensure that the interface of sites activates the public domain and invites the public into new publicly accessible spaces.
  • O8. Ensure that podiums are articulated to appear as smaller parts to create a positive fine grained and exciting experiences at street level.
  • O9. Ensure street blocks present as a group of buildings and not as a single building.
  • O10. Ensure for a common language between buildings using materials that are long lasting and need little maintenance such as masonry, face brick and natural building materials generally.
  • O11 Retain significant trees and integrate them in the design of new developments.

General controls applicable to all Key Sites

In the event of any inconsistency between this section of this chapter and other parts of this DCP, these provisions prevail to the extent of any inconsistency.

Controls

  • C1. The design and delivery of key sites will take a Country centred approach in accordance with the guidelines and controls at Section 2.3 of this Chapter.
  • C2. An Aboriginal consultant shall be engaged at the outset of the site and context analysis and throughout the design process.
  • C3. Where appropriate, refer to section 3.3 for specifications for cycleways, laneways and arcades.
  • C4. Key sites should provide up to 25% tree canopy and up to 50% green cover. Canterbury Square shall provide a minimum of 40% tree canopy cover to beautify this space and provide shade.
  • C5. Key sites will reflect the masonry heritage character of the Canterbury Local Centre through the choice of materials and finishes in development. Face brickwork and masonry and natural materials shall be used at a higher solid to void ratio. Contemporary design is invited using a palette of face brickwork, off-form concrete with timber and copper detailing. Render, Alucobond, curtain walls and glazed awnings and balustrades are not supported.
  • C6. Building articulation is to minimise different materials and colours and aim for simplicity not complexity. A response to orientation should be implemented to provide for the articulation of each façade. This can be achieved by the western facade being more closed and shaded with vertical blades to control heat, while the northern facade has deep eaves and horizontal shading and is more open to the sun.
  • C7. To mitigate urban heat, permeable paving will be used in association with understorey planting with canopy trees. Water features including misting sprays, fountains and design elements that store water should be provided. Publicly accessible laneways will be shaded as will arcades.
  • C8. Building facades should show depth and shadow and exciting detailing as shown at 4.5 and 4.6 of this Chapter.

  • P1.
  • Deliver a high quality civic square of at least 1,500m2 of public open space to anchor the development as a new civic hub for the Local Centre that works in cooperation with the new civic high street, Robert Street.   • P2. Extend Pierson Lane to the northern edge of 61-71A Jeffrey Street to replace the existing Jeffrey Lane. This will remove vehicle circulation from the northern edge of the square.
  • P3. Relocate the existing supermarket underground to maximise active uses at street level.
  • P4. Activate Canterbury Square on Jeffrey Street South and Pierson Lane, where possible with fine grain shopfronts.

  • P6. Mitigate urban heat gain in the design and material selection for the square. Use permeable paving, water features, misters and lush planting.

  • P8. Select materials and finishes that have longevity, minimal maintenance and are robust. Reinforce the heritage character in Canterbury using face brickwork and masonry.

Landscape Principles

  • P1. Ensure partnership with First Nations people in the planning and delivery of public open space.
  • P2. Minimum 40% canopy coverage across the site.
  • P3. Minimum 50% of the open space must have a minimum of 2 hours of continuous solar access.
  • P4. Minimum 50% of the site must be deep soil zone - ensure all deep soil zone are free draining and not covered, all paving within deep soil zone should be permeable.
  • P5. Include a variety of active and passive recreational activity options.
  • P6. Include a playground area of minimum 350m².
  • P7. Include an open lawn area of minimum 500m².
  • P8. Arrange the space to allow direct, clear sightlines from surrounding areas into and through the space as per CPTED design principles.
  • P9. Include public art as part of the design of the open space.

KS4- 186-206 Canterbury Road

Vision

This site is a catalyst for the Local Centre and for the southern side of Canterbury Road. Design Principles

  • P1. Create a quality outcome for the Local Centre and consider regional views by demonstrating design excellence across all levels of the development, reflecting on the Canterbury's history and materiality, its Connection to Country and establishing a celebrated presence evident in the prominence of its tallest elements.
  • P2. Set the buildings back from the Tincombe Street and Canterbury Road intersection to retain views to the Canterbury Hotel along Canterbury Road from the north and south and provide public domain enhancement to all surrounding streets. Use face brick that is complementary to the Canterbury Hotel throughout the development.

  • P4. Have greater solid to void ratios in facades to reflect Canterbury's heritage character.

  • P6. As building are visible from the open space and from Campsie Centre, particular consideration should be provided to the form and design as viewed from the wider context.
  • P7. Provide a minimum of 3m green interface setback along the boundary with adjacent sites.
  • P8. Access and service should be located along Close Street.
  • P9. Activate Canterbury with fine grain tenancies on the ground floor.
  • P10 Coordinate with TFNSW prior ot the lodgement of a DA to explore opportunities to provide servicing to the potential reuse of the heritage listed signal box along the northern boundary of the site. 3m street setback

Vision

This triangular site establishes an architectural landmark at the northern gateway of Canterbury while retaining the heritage listed police station along Canterbury Road and providing a softer interface to the residential area south and East to the site.

Design Principles

  • P1. Integrate the heritage item in the development by locating the primary building envelope along Church Street rather than Canterbury Road. This creates opportunities for landscaped courtyards framing the heritage building, enhancing and preserving its view.
  • P2. Provide upper storey setbacks and articulation to the tower and podium to address its prominent location at the northern gateway to the Local Centre and reduce visual bulk to the residential area to the east and the south.
  • P3. Deliver high quality landscape treatment that integrates the heritage item into the development and enhances its amenity.
  • P4. Provide a 3m planted buffer setback along the southern edge

This significant site is a key component to the vitality of the civic areas of the Local Centre and is located at the corner of Robert and Broughton Streets adjacent to the station. Robert Street is the primary civic street and works together with Jeffrey Street South and Square to form the Local Centre's core. Taller slender building will act as landmarks within the core which will be read from inside and outside of the Local Centre. Proposed High Street Solar access to Robert Street

Design Principles

  • P1. The site forms part of a civic street wall on the northern side of Robert Street.
  • P2. Activate the ground floor with fine grain shopfronts on both Robert and Broughton Street frontages and provide an engaging urban environment for visitors and residents.
  • P3. Provide a 3m street setback at the frontage to Robert Street to widen the street and establish well designed high amenity public domain to support the commercial activity of the shopfronts and the movement of pedestrians in the Local Centre.
  • P6. Create a slender, simply articulated tower design and 3 storey street wall to enhance solar exposure and amenity to Robert Street.

Design Principles

  • P7. Establish at a minimum, a 3m wide deep soil planting zone along the western boundary capable of supporting mature tree growth to interface with the R4 residential zone.
  • P8. Provide high quality landscape design to the ground floor and podium rooftop reflecting Connecting to Country principles, enhancing local amenity, establishing habitat, and supporting passive cooling of the environment.
  • P9. Provide a high quality communal rooftop that has planting that responds to climate and provides shade for users.

This mid-block site is at the heart of Robert Street and has the potential to set a benchmark for design quality for the Local Centre. This site works together with KS-7 to provide a civic street frontage activated by fine grained shopfronts. Uses may include hospitality, commercial and retail at street level with residential uses above to activates the Centre Core. The site will deliver a service lane on the eastern boundary to ensure the Robert Street frontage has optimal activation and pedestrian safety and that waste servicing will occur behind the development. loading to neighbouring site Proposed High Street Landscaped podium and rooftop Tallest building element Indicative Building envelope Landscaped courtyard Solar access to Robert Street 3m deep soil planting zone supporting mature tree growth

Design Principles

  • P1. Ground floor activation with fine grain shopfronts along Robert Street which turns the corner onto the service lane, Robert Lane, creates a destination and attractions to the new high street.
  • P2. A 3m street setback and public domain improvement delivers a high amenity pedestrian friendly environment supporting the vibrancy of the street.
  • P3. Establish at a minimum, a 3m wide deep soil planting zone along the western boundary capable of supporting mature tree growth to interface with the R4 residential zone.
  • P4. High quality materials and finishes reminiscent of Canterbury heritage to be utilised for the podium, retails shopfronts and public domain. Face brickwork and masonry is recommended.
  • P5. Slender built form and a 3 storey street wall enhances solar exposure and amenity to Robert Street, with a 3m upper-level setback along Robert Street and 2m upper-level setback along the new laneway.
  • P6. A 9m wide two-way service lane will be delivered along the site's eastern boundary. It will service the development and ensure the Robert Street frontages remain dedicated to commercial activity with high amenity. In the future the lane will extend as a pedestrian lane up to John Street
  • P7. Provide high quality landscape design to the podium rooftop reflecting connection to country principles, enhancing local amenity, establishing habitat, and supporting passive cooling of the urban environment.

KS9- 1-3 Close Street and 242258 Canterbury Road

Vision

To create a development with a sense of place that reflects the heritage of Canterbury Local Centre and provides an address and connection with the Cooks River.

Key Objectives

  • O1. Break down the scale of the development so it appears like several buildings.
  • O2. Integrate the development to its natural and historical context.
  • O3. Minimize the number of materials used in facade and rationalize the design.
  • O4 . Establish a positive architectural gateway to the south of the precinct.
  • O5. Establish an engaging public realm interface to Canterbury Road and Close Street.

Figure 76: Axonometric view of 1-13 Close Street and 242-258 Canterbury Road indicative massing of potential future development.

Design Principles

  • P1. Use materials that reflects Canterbury's heritage and history and responds to the proximity of the Sugar House and the Canterbury Hotel on Canterbury Road. This includes face brick, stone and concrete.
  • P2. The facade along Close Street is to appear visually broken into three different buildings, each one in a different but complimentary face brick or masonry and separated from each other by a recessed vertical indentation. Each indentation's length to depth ratio must range between 2:1 and 3:1. The total length of the two indentations must be equal to 15% or more of the total length of the Close Street facade.
  • P3. The facade along Canterbury Road is to appear visually broken into two buildings separated by one recessed vertical indentation of 1.5m depth minimum and a length to depth ratio ranging between 2:1 to 3:1.
  • P4 . A portion of the development that is visually expressed as a building, (as opposed to an indentation) must be taller than the adjacent indentations by at least 1.5m so that the visual differentiation between the buildings is also reflected in the skyline of the development and fully perceived from the public domain.
  • P5. The development must provide opportunity for rooftop communal open space that takes advantage of its prime location along the Cooks River and Lesley Muir Reserve.
  • P6. The development must provide a generous double height internal public plaza at the Close Street intersection extending further into a pedestrian connection through to the Cooks River. The plaza should be designed with high quality material finishes and landscaping, and should be sleeved with active uses on the ground floor such as cafe, restaurant, corner shop or commercial premises.
  • P7. The development should provide commercial ground floor along Canterbury Road and close street to the extent of the B2 zone.
  • P8. The landscape design and the plant selection throughout the development should reflect and take cues from the Cooks River, its history, its natural landscape and its ecology.
  • P9 If a new DA is lodged to redevelop the site, appropriate setbacks and street wall height must be considered to Canterbury Rd, close St, Lesley Muir Reserve and the Cooks River Pathway.

APPENDICES

Appendix 1- Definitions

Architectural character refers to the style, design, and general arrangement of the exterior of a building and includes articulation, composition of building elements such as but not limited to fenestration, material use and details, building entrances, balconies, balustrades, awnings, planters, pergolas, boundary walls, fences.

Annual Exceedance Probability (AEP): The chance of a flood of a given or larger size occurring in any one year, usually expressed as a percentage. For example, if a peak flood discharge of 500m3/s has an AEP of 5%, it means that there is a 5% chance (that is a onein-twenty chance) of a 500m3/s or larger event occurring in any one year.

Articulation zone applies to a tall building and means that within the street frontage length of a podium, a 1 - 1.5m deep articulation zone is provided to allow architectural form to develop. Balconies for amenity and surveillance of the street form part of this articulation zone.

Building envelope means the space that is defined by the maximum building height, gross floor area, street, side and rear setbacks and upper storey setbacks.

Destination shade is where the shaded area is the focal point.

Dynamic content sign means a small format sign that has a digital, LCD, LED, plasma or other electronic display area capable of displaying animated, variable or multimedia content and requires a continual power supply for the display area to show content.

EV Distribution Board is a distribution board dedicated to EV charging that is capable of supplying not less than 50% of EV connections at full power at any one time during off-peak periods, to ensure impacts of maximum demand are minimised, and that increases to electrical feed sizes are not required. To deliver this, the distribution board will be complete with an EV Load Management System and an active suitably sized connection to the main switchboard. The distribution board must provide adequate space for the future installation (post construction) of compact meters in or adjacent to the distribution board, to enable the body corporate to measure individual EV usage in the future.

EV Ready Connection Is a spare dedicated 32A circuit included in the EV Distribution Board to facilitate seamless future installation of cabling from an EV charger to the board, along with a circuit break-er to supply power to the circuit.

EV Load Management System is to be capable of:

  • ⚬ Reading real time current and energy from the electric vehicle chargers under management
  • ⚬ Determining, based on known installation parameters and real time data, the appropriate behaviour of each EV charger to minimise building peak power demand whilst ensuring electric vehicles connected are full recharged.
  • ⚬ Scale to include additional chargers as they are added to the site over time.

Fine Grain is architectural character and includes massing, articulation, composition of building elements including material use and details. These include building entrances, fenestration, signage, balconies, balustrades, awnings and planters at street and lane level.

Floorplate refers to the total area occupied by a single floor of a building, measured from the outer edges of the external walls. It defines the building's footprint at each level and influences factors such as structural efficiency, spatial layout, access to natural light, and overall building massing.

Front setback means a setback from a street boundary.

Green roofs (including green awnings) are roof surfaces that are partially or fully covered with vegetation are known as green roofs (or green awnings). They have a series of layers including a vegetated layer, a growing medium, and a waterproof membrane.

Incidental shade is shade experienced when passing by or through.

Isolated site is a site that has limitations on its future potential development because of its size and shape, proximity to other development and its ability to be consolidated with other properties for development purposes.

Large developments are developments with a minimum frontage of 45m of greater.

Large food waste generating businesses are premises that produce ≥660L/week of red bin capacity.

Major drainage systems: 'Overland' drainage routes, which can include roads and recreational are-as. Minor drainage systems refer to all gutters, pipes, culverts, open channels, natural creeks and other storm water infrastructure.

Maximum External Solar Reflectance is the maximum allowable percentage of solar reflectance for the external face of a Reflective Surface. The percentage of solar reflectance is to be measured at a normal angle of incidence

Non-reflective surfaces are those surfaces that diffusely reflect light and heat and for this DCP are defined as those surfaces that have a specular normal reflection of less than 5%.

Normal operations refers to all building energy requirements other than the provision of standby power generations.

Open space is hard surfaced public space within a square, courtyard or plaza as well as open parkland with landscape and play areas.

Pedestrian lanes are non-trafficable by vehicles and cyclists and are for pedestrians only. These lanes are narrower and are open to the sky but may in part be covered by awnings.

Pedestrian links are non-trafficable by vehicles and are for pedestrians only. These lanes are narrower and are predominantly open to the sky but may in part be covered by awnings or buildings.

Podium means the base of a taller building that is built close to or along the site boundary or boundaries.

Probable maximum flood (PMF): The largest flood that could conceivably occur at a particular location, usually estimated from probable maximum

Public domain are are the streets and open spaces surrounding or adjoining the site.

Publicly accessible space is located on a private site and invites the public into through site links and green spaces.

Reflective Surface Ratio (RSR) is the ratio of reflective to nonreflective external surface on any given façade.

Reflective surfaces are those surfaces that directly reflect light and heat and for this DCP are defined as those surfaces that have a specular normal reflection of greater than 5% and includes glazing, glass-faced spandrel panel, some metal finishes and high gloss finishes.

Reinforced corner is where the building corner that must address both street frontages, define and reinforce the street edge through massing and façade orientation and ties together the different street frontages and podiums. Reinforced corners may exceed the maximum podium height of connected street frontages.

Service lanes prioritise vehicles over pedestrians between 10pm7am. At other times during the day.

Shared EV Connection provides a minimum Level 2 40A fast charger and power supply to a designated car parking space, which is connected to an EV Distribution Board.

Shared lanes give pedestrians priority over vehicles and have footpaths that are level with lanes. Service vehicles use these lanes between 8pm-7am.

Solar heat reflectance is the measure of a material's ability to reflect solar radiation. A 0% solar heat reflectance means no solar heat radiation is reflected and 100% solar heat reflectance means that all of the incident solar heat radiation is reflected. In general, lighter coloured surfaces and reflective surfaces such as metals will have typically higher solar heat reflectance, with dark coloured surfaces or dull surfaces will typically have lower solar heat reflectance. External solar heat reflectance measured at the surface normal (90 degrees) is used in these controls Solar Reflectance Index (SRI) is a composite measure of a materials ability to reflect solar radiation (solar reflectance) and emit heat which has been absorbed by the material. For example, standard black paint has an SRI value of 5 and a standard white paint has an SRI value of 100. The lower the SRI value of a material, the more heat is absorbed and the hotter it will get.

Solar transmittance is the percentage of solar radiation which can pass through a material. Opaque surfaces such as concrete will have 0% solar transmittance, dark or reflective glass may have less than 10%, whilst transparent surfaces such as clear glass may allow 80 to 90% solar transmittance.

Street frontage length is the length of a podium or street wall before a lane, link, entry lobby or similar is provided.

Street wall storey height is the storey height of the building or podium. It is what defines streets, spaces and laneways.

Tall buildings are buildings that are over 50m in height.

Through-site links provide internal pedestrian and cycling connections within a building, designed to enhance accessibility and support active transport. These links should be lined with fine-grained shop fronts to activate edges and create a vibrant, engaging public interface.

Upper storey setback means the setback from a site boundary for the part of the building located above the street wall or podium. The upper storey setback controls can be applied as an 'average' across the building frontage, to enable variability in appearance.

WSUD is water sensitive urban design which is an integrated approach to urban planning and design that aims to manage and use water sustainably within the urban environment and provide for urban green spaces.

Acknowledgment of Country

The City of Canterbury-Bankstown acknowledges the traditional country of the Darug (Darag, Dharug, Daruk and Dharuk) and the Eora peoples.

We recognise and respect their cultural heritage, beliefs and relationship with the land. We acknowledge that they are of continuing importance to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples living today.

Council also acknowledges other Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander language groups in the City and works closely with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities to advance reconciliation in the City.

We're committed to creating a liveable and loveable City for all our residents

Great Cities

We believe in creating vibrant, dynamic, and diverse communities that offer opportunities for people to connect, pursue their passions, and contribute to the world around them.

Naturally Green

We protect and prioritise nature in and around our city to enhance environmental sustainability and improve the quality of life for our residents.

Design Excellence

We encourage buildings, spaces, and objects that are both beautiful and practical, enhancing the beauty, accessibility, and safety of our built environment.

People First

We prioritise the needs, preferences, and aspirations of our community in all aspects of urban planning and design, creating supportive and enriching places people love.

Community

We engage with our community to ensure their needs and aspirations are reflected in the outcome, creating sustainable, resilient, vibrant, diverse, and inclusive places.

Sustainability

We seek designs that reduce negative impacts on the environment while also promoting social and economic well-being.

Net-Zero

We encourage our community to design buildings and places that produce as much renewable energy as they consume, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, lowering energy bills, and increasing resilience to environmental shocks and stresses.

Section 1 INTRODUCTION

1.1 Application of this Chapter

This Chapter of the Canterbury-Bankstown DCP 2023, (CBDCP 2023), supports the CanterburyBankstown Local Environmental Plan 2023, (LEP), by providing additional objectives, principles and development controls to enhance the functionality, design and amenity of development within the Belmore and Lakemba Precinct, (also referred to as 'the Precinct' in this Chapter). The Precinct is comprised of two Local Centres, Belmore and Lakemba as noted in the CanterburyBankstowns Local Strategic Planning Statement.

This Chapter of the CBDCP 2023 applies to all development on the land within the Precinct as identified in Figure 2. Other Chapters, as relevant, of the CBDCP 2023 must also be addressed as part of a Development Application.

Where there is an inconsistency between the controls in this Chapter and other Chapters of the CBDCP 2023, this chapter prevails to the extent of the inconsistency except in respect of Chapter 4 Heritage.

1.2 Vision for Belmore and Lakemba Precinct

Vision

The Belmore and Lakemba Local Centres are vibrant hubs where the community can come together and celebrate their cultural diversity .

The Local Centres will provide greater housing choice that is well located to services and infrastructure to cater to the diverse needs of our communities. New buildings will be well-designed , in ways that respond to Belmore and Lakemba's unique character , providing sensitive interfaces and transitions between low-rise areas and heritage, and ensuring that new urban areas retain a human scale and community feel.

Growth in Belmore and Lakemba will be supported by enhanced public transport connections, increased retail activity and new services, new walking and cycling links and green walkable streets . Burwood Road and Haldon Streets vibrancy will be enhanced and continue to support a thriving and distinct local business community .

Investment into key parks and community infrastructure including the Belmore Sports and Recreation Precinct, Parry Park and a new community and open space area in the heart of Lakemba will ensure the community can enjoy high amenity as the Local Centres evolve over time.

1.3 How to read this DCP

This DCP Chapter is structured around a hierarchy of criteria encompassing objectives, principles and controls. The intent is to provide clear, direct and informative development controls and design guidance for all new development in the Belmore and Lakemba Precinct.

When addressing the criteria, it is important to consider the purpose of each step, as outlined on this page. Collectively these elements create a comprehensive framework that will enable the Belmore and Lakemba Precinct to deliver high quality renewal opportunities that align with the Vision for the Precinct.

Figure 4. Flowchart of DCP structure (Source: Edges Al BaroukBy Studio Toggle, Salmiya, Kuwait.

Objectives

These are the 'why' we have the principles and controls in place.

Principles

These are the 'what' we want statements. They provide clear direction as to what should be done, without saying how to do it. How these are achieved comes down to individual site circumstances, design and merit.

Controls

These state to the applicant 'how' to achieve the objectives and principles. They are clear and measurable standards to guide development.

Section 2 UNDERSTANDING PLACE

2.1 Structure Plan

The Structure Plan provides an overview of the intended outcomes for the Precinct. The Structure Plan has been informed by analysis of the opportunities and constraints for the Local Centres. These opportunities include the desired land uses, built form character, housing types, open space, streetscape improvements and pedestrian and cycling connections.

Key elements of the Structure Plan consist of:

  • ⚬ Enhance the vibrant high streets on Haldon Street and Burwood Road to support street life, retail activity and cultural expression.
  • ⚬ High rise urban living focused around and between Belmore and Lakemba Metro stations.
  • ⚬ New and enhanced parks and plazas.
  • ⚬ New social infrastructure that supports a growing community.
  • ⚬ Green connections, shared lanes and pedestrian links that support walking and cycling in key locations.
  • ⚬ Increased tree canopy and green cover to create cool, green and attractive neighbourhoods and to reduce urban heat gain.
  • ⚬ High quality built form outcomes based on robust design and planning and reflective of existing character.

The Structure Plan is shown in Figure 6.

Objectives

  • O1. To provide an overview of the intended outcomes for the Belmore and Lakemba Precinct.

Principles

  • P1. Development should align with the overarching elements of the Structure Plan, as shown in Figure 6.

2.2 Character Areas

The Belmore and Lakemba Precinct will be comprised of different areas of distinct character. Through detailed analysis, seven character areas have been identified. Applicants are to identify which character area that the development site is located in and be cognisant of the key attributes of the existing context, where relevant, and the desired future context for the character area.

Objectives

  • O1. To achieve the desired future character of the Belmore and Lakemba Precincts and guide development to deliver this desired character.

Controls

  • C1. Development must consider and address the outcomes expressed in the character area statements and principles.
  • C2. Development Applications must be accompanied by a site and context analysis plan that demonstrates an understanding of the manner a site integrates and is consistent with the desired future character area.

Desired Future Character Areas

2.2.1 Lakemba High Street

The Lakemba High Street character area will have its vibrant multicultural identity enhanced, offering a dynamic mix of shopping, dining and community services, alongside new housing to support a thriving atmosphere day and night.

Building on the success of the Ramadan Markets, Haldon Street will be prioritised as a pedestrianised space lined with vibrant retail uses that activate the street level, complemented by shoptop housing above to create a lively civic area.

The bulk and scale of new development will reflect the predominant 2 to 3 storey street wall height in Haldon Street and the parapet character, with fine grain tenancies incorporating masonry and brick. Where possible, pre 1950 shop facades will be retained and sympathetically restored. Additional storeys will be setback on a podium, featuring green terraces and balconies.

Figure 10. Axonometric view of Lakemba High Street with indicative massing of potential future development and photo of Haldon Street's fine grain retail with shoptop housing.

As the cultural heart of Lakemba, the character area will feature high-quality public spaces that encourages exploration and social interaction. The character area surrounds the Metro station and the enhanced public space and aims to meet diverse community needs while promoting entertainment, convenience, and connectivity.

KS-1 and 2 will provide new and enhanced public space and links at ground level, supported by higher-density developments. Specifically, KS-2, the Quigg Street block, will be revitalised to include a new central open space with the opportunity for consolidated community facilities, while on KS-1, Jubilee Reserve will be expanded and improved.

Gillies Lane behind Haldon Street will be designed to balance service needs with pedestrian amenity. An attractive and safe interface to open space and community facilities will be provided at Quigg Street. An improved and widened pedestrian link between Haldon Street and Gillies Lane will link this key site to Haldon Street.

Darling Square in Haymarket is a lively, pedestrian friendly place that seamlessly integrates retail, dining, residential and community gathering spaces. This dynamic area features a blend of mixed-use developments, thoughtfully designed and activated pedestrian links and an iconic library building, all centered around a green open space that serves as the heart of the community (Source: Architectus)

Fine grained shoptop housing, Nightingale, Marrickville, Sydney (Source: Tom Roe)

Activated sunny retail strip, The Corso, Manly, (Source: Architectus)

Activated shared laneway, Birdwood Lane, Lane Cove (Source: Architectus)

Principles

  • P1. Built form along Haldon Street: New developments on Haldon Street should retain the existing high street character by:
  • Maintaining a street wall height of 2 to 3 storeys in line with the predominant existing building height. New development should be consistent with the solid to void ratios in historic shopfront masonry buildings, awnings, parapets and windows. Refer to Section 4.2.3 Street wall.
  • Retaining and integrating pre 1950 shopfront facades sympathetically into the design of new development, including restoration and removal of any uncharacteristic and intrusive features.
  • Reinforcing fine-grain active frontages with glazing and openings that invigorate Haldon Street, fostering a lively atmosphere and creating a dynamic pedestrian environment, whilst also protecting residents from potential noise generation. Refer to Section 4.3.2 Active street frontages and edges.
  • Using traditional materials such as brickwork and masonry that reflect the area's heritage and pre 1950s facades. Refer to Section 4.5 Materials and finishes.
  • Setting back upper levels to provide green podium communal spaces and passive surveillance opportunities. Refer to Section 4.6 Communal and podium open space. 2
  • P2. Lanes: Lanes behind Haldon Street will be enhanced to support pedestrians and cyclists amenity while also accommodating service vehicles and driveways creating a high amenity network that promotes safety and accessibility for all users. Refer to Section 3.3 Streets, shared lanes, pedestrian links and arcades. Development interfacing laneways should:
  • For commercial uses: consider opportunities for active lane edges, including cafes, outdoor seating, planters and where possible deep soil.
  • For residential uses: provide high quality landscaping, deep soil and apartments with private entries.
  • P3. Key sites (KS-1 Jubilee Reserve and KS-2 Quigg Street): Development at Jubilee Reserve and the Quigg Street key sites must deliver improved permeability, new open space and active street and lane interfaces. These sites are identified as key catalysts for community infrastructure and access. Refer to Section 6 Key Sites. 3
  • P4. Pedestrian link between Haldon Street and Gillies Lane: A widened open-air link between Haldon Street and Gillies Lane is to be delivered with active frontages, including retail and café seating, lighting, and planting, to create a vibrant, safe, and well-used connection.

Desired Future Character Areas

2.2.2 Belmore High Street

The Belmore High Street character area will be revitalised and showcase a diverse mix of retail and urban services, complemented by new residential developments that enhance the area's liveliness and appeal.

The character area will feature an improved pedestrian environment and activated shared lanes, making it more accessible and attractive for walking and cycling in and around the new Metro station. The local services and shops will provide convenient amenities.

Enhancements to Burwood Road will prioritise the pedestrian experience, incorporating traffic calming measures and urban greening while maintaining essential north-south transport connections for vehicles and buses.

Burwood Road will maintain a diverse mix of retail and commercial services, complemented by residential apartments above. A 2-3 storey street wall characterised by brick and masonry finishes will define the architectural identity of the area with additional storeys set back to enhance the traditional streetscape. Pre 1950 shop facades will be retained and sympathetically integrated into new development.

Figure 11. Axonometric view of Belmore High Street with indicative massing of potential future development.

Shared lanes will facilitate service vehicle access while improving the pedestrian and cycling network creating opportunities for retail activation behind Burwood Road. Enhanced pathways, greenery and cycling connections along the railway line and Leylands Parade will link this character area to key destinations, including the Metro station, Belmore Sports and Recreation Precinct and higher density residential areas between Belmore and Lakemba.

The Canterbury Leagues Club key site is a significant attraction within the Belmore Local Centre and represents a substantial landholding strategically located near the station. This site presents a significant opportunity to catalyse Belmore Local Centre, through mixed use development with high rise apartments. It will feature pedestrian friendly links and shared lanes, improved interfaces and greening as well as a new publicly accessible open space that will serve as a green focal point, with activated edges to encourage community gathering, enjoyment and amenity.

Figure 12. Illustration of enhanced lanes behind Burwood Road that manage rear retail and residential frontages. Setbacks to retail accommodate servicing, driveways as well as incidental active edges and landscaping. Setbacks to residential are for landscaped garden apartments.

Principles

  • P1. Built Form along Burwood Road: New developments along Burwood Road should retain and enhance the fine-grain traditional high street character by:
  • Maintaining a street wall height of 2-3 storeys that aligns with the predominant existing building height and architectural detailing including solid to void ratios, awnings, parapets and windows. See Section 4.2.3 Street wall.
  • Retaining pre 1950 shop facades and sympathetically integrating them into the design of new development. Key elements such as the historic paraphets and awnings should be restored and uncharacteristic and intrusive features removed.
  • Fostering the fine-grain active street frontages with glazing and openings that animate Burwood Road at street level. Mitigate noise and create a lively pedestrian atmosphere. See Section 4.3.2 Active street frontage and edges.
  • Using materials that reflect the traditional face brickwork and masonry of surrounding buildings including heritage and pre 1950 facades. See Section 4.5 Materials and finishes.

  • Setting back the upper levels above the street wall to provide green podium communal spaces and passive surveillance. See Section 4.6 Rooftop and communal open space.
  • P2. Lanes: Lanes will be enhanced to better accommodate pedestrians and cyclists, while also facilitating service vehicles and driveways, creating a high-amenity network that promotes safety and accessibility for all users.
  • P3. Development interfacing lanes should manage servicing and driveway access within setbacks while also providing increased amenity, activity and greening. Specifically:
  • For commercial uses, consider opportunities for active lane edges, including cafes, outdoor seating, planters and where possible deep soil.
  • For residential uses, provide high quality landscaping, deep soil, and apartments with private entries. Refer to Section 3.3 Streets, shared lanes, pedestrian links and arcades.
  • P4. The Leagues Club key site; development on this site must provide improved permeability, active edges to streets and shared lanes and deliver new open space, as identified the KS-3 plan. See Section 6 Key Sites.

Desired Future Character Areas

2.2.3 Urban living

The Urban living character area will offer architecturally inspiring apartments within slender towers on podiums that create a varied skyline and contribute to a high quality public domain and streetscape.

The area will feature green streets, well-connected pedestrian and cycle links, along with inviting public space. This design aims to cultivate a vibrant, walkable urban neighbourhood conveniently located near transport, services and amenity.

This character area will experience substantial revitalisation, featuring new apartment developments primarily ranging from 9 to 15 storeys with a four to five storey street wall that integrates with the surroundings. Key sites will facilitate highquality developments that offer additional public benefits, including new publicly accessible open spaces and pedestrian links, enhancing the public domain and connectivity for everyone. Corner sites will be designed to accommodate landmark towers and focal points in the street.

While parts of this neighbourhood have existing residential flat buildings, others consist of detached dwellings. New development will need to consider both contexts, providing appropriate setbacks, landscaping and articulated built form.

Figure 13. Axonometric view of Urban living with indicative massing of potential future development and typical typologies.

N

New developments will prioritise direct street access and landscaped private open space within setbacks for ground-floor apartments and terraces, encouraging passive surveillance of the streets, pedestrian links and shared lanes. Apartments adjacent to open space will be designed to provide a high quality interface and frontage to parks. Podiums and rooftops will offer opportunities to contribute to urban greening and communal open space for residents.

This neighbourhood benefits from a wellestablished tree canopy along Leylands Parade, offering shade, biodiversity and a beautiful green streetscape. New tree canopy will be focused along key streets including Wangee Road, Lakemba Street and The Boulevarde. This will contribute to a cool, green and attractive network of streets. Additionally, proposed cycleways along key streets will offer a safe, convenient and healthy way to navigate the neighbourhood while connecting to the new east-west Sydney Metro pedestrian link.

Development adjacent to public open space will be orientated to face the park, maximise park outlook from living areas and balconies and create a positive interface that promotes passive surveillance through entrances, balconies, terraces, and high quality landscaping. See Section 3.3 Streets, shared lanes, pedestrian links and arcades.

  • P5. Elegant towers set upon podiums will feature facades that respond to orientation, expose concrete structure and are responsive to the context using face brickwork. Podiums will include articulation and breaks to ensure they don't overwhelm the streetscape. See Section 4.2.1 Building height and storeys and 4.4 Visual diversity, articulation and fine grain.
  • P6. The use of brick and masonry will integrate with the existing brick character of the neighbourhood. High quality finishes and textures should be provided at street level. See Section 4.5 Materials and finishes.

Limiting driveway crossovers through placing them next to each other or in rear laneways will enhance walkability and amenity in the area, contributing to a greener and shadier environment allowing for more landscaping and tree canopy along the streets and in setbacks.

2.2.6 Canterbury Road

The Canterbury Road character area will remain as a vital vehicle connection continuing to provide employment and services for the local area, while also offering opportunities for improved amenity, greening and alternate connections to make the area more attractive and pedestrian and cyclist friendly.

The character area will primarily showcase medium-format commercial and retail developments, alongside mixed-use buildings that are 6 to 8 storeys. Additionally, this area contains lower-scale public buildings, such as Belmore South Public School and St Joseph's Catholic Church and School, as well as low-scale dwellings that are expected to remain as low density. This will create a diversity of scales and uses that requires careful consideration of interfaces.

Desired Future Character Areas

2.2.7 Industrial lands

The industrial land character areas play a vital role in supporting the local economy by offering employment opportunities and essential services. There are two character areas.

The Punchbowl Road Industrial area features medium-scale, low-rise light industrial uses with direct access to Punchbowl Road, connecting to larger employment lands in Greenacre and Enfield. This area is well-established and situated at the northern periphery of the Precinct. By contrast, the Lakemba Street Industrial area is a smaller, fine grain cluster of light industrial tenancies embedded within the residential context.

There is a strong commitment to preserving existing industrial zoned land with unchanged controls. As the surrounding context evolves, a sensitive and functional interface between industrial lands and residential areas will be essential for ensuring for amenity and mitigating impacts.

In particular, the Lakemba Street Industrial area presents opportunities to enhance streetscape amenity through tree planting, landscaping, and the introduction of pedestrian and cycle friendly improvements linking Belmore and Lakemba Stations. Over time, tenancies could incorporate complementary uses such as cafés or other local retail offers to activate the street and contribute to a more walkable neighbourhood.

Redevelopment of industrial sites should prioritise:

  • ⚬ Improving the public domain and mitigating urban heat outcomes through landscaping, permeable paving and tree canopy planting;
  • ⚬ Reduction of building bulk through modulation of the building envelope and improvement in design quality;
  • ⚬ Simplicity in design using quality materials;
  • ⚬ Minimal quality signage;
  • ⚬ Sustainable design and operation; and
  • ⚬ Safe, legible access for pedestrians, cyclists and service vehicles.
